subsubtopic: PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT FOR SHIPS BUILT IN COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion. At the present time ships built by offshore countries and plying their services completely in Canadian waters are subject to a 25 per cent duty. However, this duty does not apply to ships built in Commonwealth countries. This has created considerable hardship and unfair competition for the Canadian shipbuilding industry, which is having a difficult time as it is competing for contracts with these countries, that give a greater subsidization to their industry than does Canada. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the government take the necessary steps to change the Canada Shipping Act and remove this preferential treatment which has been an anachronism for many years.

Facilitate the selective reduction and transfer of prison populations to provide for the establishment of civilian internment camps.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 concerning the government's urea formaldehyde foam insulation policy. The government's UFFI aid policy for victims of urea formaldehyde poisoning is completely inadequate because it is a token remedy for a serious problem the government now admits it created; it fails even to begin to help thousands of Canadians who must rid their homes of UFFI; it will bring serious financial hardship to home owners who are now left with properties that have little or no resale value, and it arbitrarily sets a suspect gas level without considering the different reactions by thousands of Canadians who are and will be exposed to UFFI. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae):

That the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources reassign funds now allocated for CHIP to insulate homes this year and next and make these moneys available for an emergency fund to assist all UFFI victims with the costs of removing this foam and restoring their homes to previous condition.

Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas there are thousands of freshwater fishermen across Canada who are obliged to make unemployment insurance contributions but who, at the same time, are unable to collect benefits under this program because their season does not coincide with that of saltwater fishermen, and whereas not only is this situation grossly unfair it is also causing undue hardship for those thousands of fishermen unable to find work in the off-season due to the disastrous state of the economy under this Liberal government, and who are suffering, like all Canadians, from the effects of the government's high interest rate policies, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper):

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REQUEST THAT TERMS BE OBSERVED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the new Minister of State for International Trade. In Canada today there are 50,000 auto workers on lay-off, 21,000 of whom are not likely ever to be able to return to their jobs. Because of the failure of the minister's predecessors in Industry, Trade and Commerce to insist that the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact be lived up to, we have 15,000 fewer jobs than we ought to have. Will the minister take immediate steps in exercising his responsibility to ensure that this pact is lived up to so those 15,000 Canadians who ought to have jobs in this industry, because of that pact, will get them?

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REQUEST THAT TERMS BE OBSERVED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first of all, 1 would like to say that no one has ever worked harder for the Canadian automobile industry than my colleague, the hon. member for Windsor West.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want to try to clear up the most recent fraud the Minister of Finance is trying to perpetrate on the Canadian public.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION ON TAX EXEMPTIONS
speechtext: In admitting now that the basis for his claiming to reduce taxes is that he has kept in place the indexing proposal, the minister is saying that he has cut taxes by leaving in place an element of the tax system which was already there. speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION ON TAX EXEMPTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just to clear up the first point, I have said that the basis of my claim that there has been a very substantial tax cut amounting in deductions to $3 billion this year is not entirely indexation. That is part of it. There is also the reduction in the marginal tax rate, and there is also the reduction in the federal tax credit, which has benefited and will benefit over a million low and medium-income families in Canada. Taken together, the indexation, the cuts in the marginal tax rates, and the restructuring of the federal tax credit, that is the total basis.
I am not forecasting what arguments might be necessary in the future to meet the rather erroneous position taken by the Leader of the Opposition this morning, yesterday, the day before yesterday, and probably on into the future.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS CALCULATION OF PROVINCIAL REVENUES
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS CALCULATION OF PROVINCIAL REVENUES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. A front-page story by Andrew Szende in the Toronto Star this morning reports revised Department of Finance calculations that provincial revenues for health, post-secondary education and other services will be slashed on a net basis by $4.5 billion over the next five years. That estimate is twice the size of the one contained in the minister's budget when he brought it down on November 12.
Will the minister confirm those revised calculations, and will he not admit that the new figures will almost definitely force the provinces to cut back substantially vital services to their

people and to increase taxes in order to cope with the shortfall?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS CALCULATION OF PROVINCIAL REVENUES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 have not had an opportunity to examine that particular article; therefore, I cannot comment on the figures quoted. However, it is my contention that the proposals which I have placed before the provinces will improve the fiscal position of the provinces each year during the course of that five-year period. Even with the proposed elimination of the revenue guarantee, for each province, taking into account the total transfers there will be and the tax offsets which were provided in the budget, these transfers will grow on an annual basis quite significantly.

The matter proposed for discussion must relate to a genuine emergency, calling for immediate and urgent consideration;-

The House resumed, from Wednesday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Whelan that Bill C-85 to establish a corporation called Canagrex to promote, facilitate and engage in the export of agricultural and food products from Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday I had the opportunity to make a few comments with respect to this bill. I understand that I have about 36 minutes left in which to make my remarks.
Last Wednesday the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) attempted to table a statement in this House listing the accomplishments of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). He said there were some 50 items on the list. I suggest that if the minister's list of accomplishments were so lengthy, the farming community would be shouting from the rooftops, "How great thou art, Mr. Minister". However, I have not heard the farming community shouting such exhorta-

January 29, 1982
Canagrex Act
tions; it will not, because the agricultural community in Canada is in very serious trouble.
There is nothing at all in the budget to help alleviate the situation. Of course, the Minister of Agriculture will say that there are some changes in the Farm Credit Corporation Act which will provide $50 million for those farmers and producers who are in trouble. That $50 million is only a drop in the bucket.
The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will suggest that the changes to provide for the Small Business Development Bond are such that they will help those farmers who are in trouble; but the banks are simply not lending on the Small Business Development Bond because the terms set down by this government are such that a borrower must be in serious financial difficulty. There is no government guarantee on a small business development bond and, for that reason, the banks look at the borrower, the individual who is in trouble, and treat the individual in the same manner as they would any other borrower. If he is in financial difficulty, and the chances are that he will be unable to pay the loan, he cannot benefit from that bond.
Why is agriculture in trouble? First of all, it is in trouble because of the high interest rates created by this government. Even the Farm Credit Corporation rate of 16.75 per cent is an unbearable burden. The bank rates, of course, are higher than 16.75 per cent. They are in the neighbourhood of 20 per cent, 21 per cent or 22 per cent.
What does this mean to the farmer? It means that if a farmer is buying land at, say, $1,000 an acre, which is not an unusual or unrealistic price as much land in the prairies is being sold for more than $1,000 an acre, and with the Farm Credit Corporation interest rate of 16.75 per cent, this farmer will have to pay $167.50 a year in interest on each acre. Most farmers in the west, because of climatic conditions, operate their farms on a two-year rotation: one year of summerfallow and one year of crop. In other words, one must produce a sufficient amount on one acre to pay the interest on two acres. Therefore, at 16.75 per cent interest, one must produce $335 on one acre to pay the interest on two acres. If one relates that to the price of grain today, which is approximately $6 a bushel, that means that one must produce 50 bushels to the acre in order to pay the interest costs.
However, on top of one's interest costs, one must pay back part of the capital. Where does that come from? Then, of course, one has input costs. Input costs and interest rates are killing the farmer today. Over the Christmas holidays, I spoke to a farmer who farms north of Moose Jaw. He told me that without taking fertilizer and crop sprays into consideration, his input costs are over $50 an acre. He must produce almost another ten bushels to the acre to pay the input costs, and these input costs are going up.
What will happen to the farmer? What will happen is that, as a result of the budget, we will see the end of the family farm. The budget will sound its death knell. Under the budget provisions, with the elimination of the IAACs, the elimination of the reserve provisions and the requirement to pay the capital
gains tax up front, I suggest there will be a situation where the family farm will not and cannot be passed on in the family. The result will be that there will be cash sales only. Who will be able to buy this land if the cost of interest and the input costs are such that one cannot produce a sufficient amount to pay the price of the land? I suggest that the only way the land can be sold will be to the land bank, to the government or to large corporations.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: It certainly won't be to a farmer.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: That is right. If the land ends up in the land bank or in the hands of the government, we will have a country of tenant farmers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Communes.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Or communes, as my colleague said. I think the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues would like to see this happen, because over the years the minister has spent a great deal of time discussing and promoting supply management. If farmers in Saskatchewan, for example, become tenants of the government and the land bank, it will be no problem for the state to control production, supply, price or the selling of these products.
Canagrex would be an ideal vehicle for the minister under these circumstances. Let us look at Clause 14 of the bill, it is fairly lengthy. The clause sets out the powers of the corporation. I quote 14(1):
Canagrex is established for the purposes of promoting, facilitating and engaging in the export of agricultural products and services and food products and services from Canada to other countries by means of the financial and other powers provided in this act, and for such purposes Canagrex may
(a)	purchase agricultural products and food products and package, process,
store, ship, insure, import, export or sell or otherwise dispose of products
purchased by it;
It is not a selling agency. It can do almost anything. It can enter into joint ventures with individuals or corporations. Subclause (g) states that Canagrex can:
-purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and hold real and personal property-
Is that clause in the bill for the purpose of giving the government the power to acquire farm land when the farmer cannot pass it on to his family? Is that what it is for? I thought Canagrex was a selling agency to facilitate the selling of agricultural products, but it is wide open. This is unbelievable. It can get involved as a corporation in every aspect of agriculture.
There is a pattern emerging, one which started to emerge in 1968 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. Since that time there has been a move away from the free enterprise system, a system which the Liberal Party espoused in those days. It was a system which was serving us well.
I thought that in the years following 1968 we were being led toward a socialist system, but recently I have had serious doubts. What is happening is we are moving toward an elitist
January 29, 1982

system of government, a system of strict government control. This bill is one of the aspects of this government control. Is it a nationalist-socialist system or a move toward the fascist state? I think members opposite would be wise to sit down and consider what is happening in their party and what is happening to our country.
1 notice some smiles on the other side. All one has to do if one is pondering what is happening is to consider the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which was passed by resolution in this House and which is now in England, provides for freedom of speech, freedom of religion and freedom of the press. The hon. member across the way nods. If he reads further in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, he will find that the federal government and every provincial government in the country can take away our freedom of speech, freedom of religion and freedom of the press.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: What does that have to do with this bill?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
I suggest this is part of the pattern and design that is taking place. It is the government which passes orders in council and in the event of an emergency, whether there is war or not, allows the release of prisoners and provides for the operation of civilian internment camps.
Let us look at the pattern that is evolving. I suggest the man at the helm knows, but at the moment the passengers on the mythical boat which the Prime Minister spoke about several years ago do not know on what shore they will land.
In May, 1976, a well-known figure in the agricultural field, Alf Presber, prepared a paper with respect to marketing. I have a copy of it. It is entitled "Summary of a Proposal for a Foreign Agricultural Marketing Service in Canada". He lists the objectives. I gather he was concerned about the fact that there had been a splinter approach developing with respect to sales of agricultural products in our country. The provinces were involved and the federal government was involved. He felt a program should be developed to deal with the situation. He suggested a foreign agricultural marketing service for Canada which would be made up of a few key individuals. I will summarize the terms of reference. I quote:
(a)	To bring about effective contact between the Canadian seller of agricultural commodities and prospective foreign buyers
(b)	To initiate sales and sales promotion projects as a co-operative effort between the Canadian seller, industry in general, trade and government(s)
(c)	To attract foreign agricultural processing technique and. . . foreign investment into Canadian agriculture;
(d)	to ascertain and to report in the fastest possible way, if necessary directly to Canadian sales organizations, on marketing opportunities for Canadian primary and processed agricultural products;
(e)	To specialize in the analysis of existing tariff and trade barriers and to search out ways to overcome such barriers;
He saw that this little group of key individuals stationed in various parts of the world with their finger on the pulse could report directly to the Department of Agriculture. He envisaged that eventually there would be a corporation set up like Canagrex to carry out these sales. He said and I quote:
Canagrex Act
The overriding purposes of the foreign agricultural marketing service in Canada is sales-
As far as I am concerned, Canagrex as a corporation should be concerned directly in sales, in co-ordinating sales with foreign governments and the industry in Canada.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that a few days ago there was an article in The Globe and Mail, on January 27, written by Kevin Cox. The headline read "Public misled on export plan, agriculture officials tell Ottawa." 1 will read one or two excerpts from that article. Mr. Cox writes:
The federal Agriculture Department has been accused of misleading the public into thinking there is widespread support for a proposed national agricultural export company.
Agricultural marketing officials from eight provinces have recommended the federal government abandon its plan for the export firm, Canagrex, saying the country lacks the personnel and the finances for such a venture.
It goes on to say that:
The controversy is complicated by the fact that the provincial ministers of agriculture say they support the Canagrex plan, even while in many cases their own marketing directors oppose it.
The article goes on to quote the marketing directors as saying that "State trading is not a general practice in developed countries and is not acceptable to most Canadians." This is the reason the Minister of Agriculture puts forward for Canagrex. He says that we need state to state trading. However, this group involved in agricultural marketing says that is not so.
It is interesting to note that the article goes on to say that Saskatchewan also supported the critique which was in opposition to the government's proposed program of Canagrex, "-fearing that Canagrex might displace provincial marketing boards which export pork and other products."
It seems to me that the critique expresses the concern of Mr. Presber, who said that the sales programs have been splintered because of provincial and federal involvement. It seems to me that effective selling requires the co-operation of the federal and provincial departments of agriculture, the producer and private business with the necessary leadership to bring these groups together, a leadership which the present Minister of Agriculture has not shown.
1 suggest that while the basic concept of this bill is sound, namely, a Crown corporation which would fill in the gap where necessary to encourage or make sales which would not otherwise be made, the bill as it now stands is too all-encompassing. The reason for this is that the name of the game should be sales. It should not be processing, it should not be packaging. The agency should not be involved in joint ventures or the acquiring of land for the purpose of leasing it out. It should deal with sales.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that when this bill goes to committee it should be given substantial consideration. The committee should be able to have before it as witnesses provincial representatives to give the provincial viewpoint, industrial representatives to give their views and the Minister

January 29, 1982
Canagrex Act
of Agriculture should be prepared to accept proposals for amendments, setting aside politics, so that this bill can be effective.
This is not what generally happens in committee or in the House. No matter how valid a suggestion for an amendment may be, when presented by a member of the opposition it is ruled out because the person submitting the amendment or making the suggestion might gain some political points.
I think that the minister was elated when an amendment I proposed before Christmas to include lamb in the meat import bill was ruled out of order on the basis that lamb was not meat.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: It is fish.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: It is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that this time around the minister is big enough-and I do not mean physically-to accept recommendations not only from provincial or private industry representatives, but from opposition and individual Members of Parliament, regardless of their political affiliation. It is my hope that if an individual Member of Parliament proposes an amendment which will effectively improve the bill, the minister will be man enough to accept that amendment. As far as I am concerned, the problems faced by the agricultural industry today are far beyond party politics. Unless there is co-operation between parties, unless there is co-operation between governments, we will not solve the problems which are facing us today. I know that all the producers in western Canada, as well as I, do not want to end up in a situation in which the government owns all the land and the producers are tenant farmers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on this bill to establish an agricultural exporting agency, Bill C-85.
At the outset, I want to say that the establishment of an agency such as this is a measure which our party supports and has urged for a long time. Canada should have a corporation that is involved solely with the promotion and export of agricultural products around the world.
My only concern is that too often an excellent proposal for a program in this country is spoiled by the people or the agency running it. It is important that we analyse the bill before us very carefully to ensure that the agency which is created is not destroyed by some bureaucrats who have no idea how to operate the agricultural economy of this country. I suggest that we try to democratize the people that run the agency as much as possible from the beginning, to make it a truly federal exporting agency. It should not be run solely by the federal government and its bureaucrats in Agriculture Canada.
For example, Clause 3 provides for a board of directors made up of a chairman, vice-chairman, president and eight other members. I suggest we should look into the possibility of amending Clause 3 which states that the federal government alone shall appoint the eight directors who will run the agency, to include a written guarantee that some of those directors shall come from the agricultural community, the farmers
themselves. The Board should include some members from private industry, and some from the federal government, of course, because that is important. Incidentally, I would point out to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) that not only private industry but many agencies are involved in agriculture, such as Intercontinental Packers Limited in Saskatchewan which are publicly owned. They should also play a role in the direction of the board.
There should also be representatives of the provinces on the board. Under our Constitution the federal and provincial governments have concurrent jurisdiction over agriculture. It has been that way since 1867, and when we set up an agency to export our agricultural products, we must reflect that reality in the agency. Because if we do not, we may have some conflict with the many dozens of provincial marketing boards which exist in each and every single province of this great country of ours.
My first suggestion is that the directors come from four different groups. There should be federal government appointees, provincial government appointees and representatives of producers and the industry, so that we have an agency that is truly federative, truly national and truly reflective of the reality of our country and of agriculture in the country.
I think it is appropriate that the agency have the powers it is being given. The hon. member for Moose Jaw was concerned about the extensive powers of the export agency. He referred to the powers of the agency respecting entering into joint ventures, signing contracts, storing products and so forth. Those powers are very extensive but I think the agency needs them. We are dealing in a highly competitive world today. Other export agencies and state agencies in other countries make sure that their exporters have the power and flexibility they need to make decisions so that they do not have to come back to their parliaments time and time again because circumstances change and are different for various agricultural products. However, in the exercise of the powers of this agency it is important that the directors operating the agency know what powers to use and how to use them, and that they use them in the interests of the farmers and the agricultural business of this country. Those powers should not be exercised solely by a few bureaucrats centrally located in Ottawa who are not sensitive to the agricultural community.
In terms of financing, I think $12.3 million for three years is probably less than the agency should have, but at least it is a start on something which is a very good idea.
In terms of the production of agricultural products, we in this country have a long way to go. We must examine the basic facts. About 40 per cent to 45 per cent of our agricultural goods are produced for export. Most of our exports are grain and oil seeds from western Canada. In 1980 we exported some $8 billion worth of food and agricultural products from Canada and imported some $5 billion worth of agricultural products and food. One of the tragedies associated with imports into this country is that many of the products we
January 29, 1982

import are products we could be producing right here. We could be providing jobs for farmers, income for Canadians, support for the Canadian dollar and jobs for workers in processing the foods we could be growing right here in this country.
One of the tragedies associated with our agricultural exports is the same tragedy associated with other exports such as oil and energy. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) talked about this. We tend to export unprocessed basic raw materials. I will give one example. We produce pork in huge factory-like processes and export it en masse from Canada. This provides very little real economic benefit and few jobs. We should be processing more food products. We should be processing labour-intensive products. This would help solve the unemployment problem we have.
I do not have current statistics on the production of food in Canada, but much research has been undertaken by Agriculture Canada, by GATT-Fly, by churches and by other organizations. If we do not smarten up, by the end of this century Canada will be a net importer of food. We will not be able to feed ourselves. In a country with a small population but a large geographic area, I think that is a crime in the twentieth century.
The Ontario Federation of Agriculture said the other day that about 26 acres of farm land goes out of production in the province of Ontario every day. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) is very familiar with what has happened in the Niagara region of Ontario, where farm land has been paved over for city suburbs, freeways, hydro lines and parks. Those developments could be undertaken a few miles away from good agricultural land, on land which cannot be used for agricultural purposes.
According to statistics we are no longer self-sufficient in many products in which we were self-sufficient in the past. Many fruits once grown in Ontario are no longer produced here but are imported from the United States and other countries around the world. There have been massive losses in the peach industry, the grape industry, the apricot industry, the pear industry, the plum industry and the vegetable industry. This is happening not only in Ontario but also in the provinces of Quebec, British Columbia and other provinces. We now produce only 18 per cent of the peaches we eat in Canada. At one time we produced the majority of peaches consumed here.
In conjunction with the export agency we are establishing, we should be looking to a national agricultural plan and the kinds of products we could be producing but are not producing in Canada. There are specialty crops we should be producing right across the country. On the prairies we could be producing for export much larger volumes of peas and faba beans. These could be exported to many countries around the world. In British Columbia we could be producing much larger volumes of fruits and vegetables. In Ontario and Quebec we could be producing and exporting more maple syrup. A few days ago one of the members of this House from Quebec spoke in the House about the export potential for maple syrup that
Canagrex Act
there is in many countries around the world. The northeastern part of the United States is probably getting some of the markets we could have. This is a job for the new export agency we are setting up. It should try to promote some of these specialty crops. We should look at the possibility of producing more mushrooms and aflatoxin-free peanuts in this country. There are cole crops in the maritimes. Some other crops are potatoes and seed potatoes. We produce specialty cattle, purebred cattle and chickens. There are all kinds of animals and livestock we could be producing and exporting to other countries around the world. I think it is important that the board of directors and the people who run the export agency are aware that they have to get out there and be aggressive and devise- along with the Parliament of Canada and the provinces-a national agricultural plan so that we can do just that.
I want to sound one note of caution. I hope the new export agency we are setting up will not try to do what our friend Jack Horner did a few years ago, and that is to export infant feeding formulas to the Third World or South America. I do not think that is the job of an export agency of this kind. It is not the job of an export agency to try to set up huge bakeries in places like Tanzania, which we have done in the past, so that they will import Canadian wheat and put local people out of work. The job of an export agency is to make sure that when we export something to other countries, especially the developing countries of the Third World, we help those countries to help themselves become self-sufficient. We should give them some of the technology they need. We should not destroy their local markets. We should not be importing products from their best farm land which are not necessary for consumption in this country. Time and time again we have imported from countries in Africa and South America crops like peanuts, tobacco and cotton produced on the best farm land in the Third World, while the people living right next door are going hungry and dying of starvation and malnutrition. We must make sure our export agency is sensitive to some of the problems of the developing world and that we do not repeat some of the historical mistakes of this government and other governments.
I see that it is one o'clock. Perhaps I could resume at two o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few more minutes to deal with this bill. Some hon. members have expressed concern about farm size and about farm land disappearing in this country. I have in front of me a copy of the GATT-Fly magazine issued a few years ago. That organiza-
14474

January 29, 1982

tion did a fair amount of research into the problem of diminishing farm land, the fact that farms are becoming larger and larger and that as a consequence there are fewer of them.
In 1951 the average farm size in this country was 113 hectares and in 1971 it was 188 hectares, which is an increase of 66 per cent.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: How big is a hectare?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
A hectare, for the information of the Conservative member, is about 2.5 acres. I do not have the statistics for 1982 but we have a similar projection which shows that the size of the farms have jumped by a corresponding 40 per cent, 50 per cent or 60 per cent.
As we make advances in technology and agriculture, I suppose it is normal that the size of farms will increase. As a farm boy from the prairies, however, I know that many farms are far too large at the present time. In many cases this is because people have more money and so they are buying more land, as are large corporations. But beyond a certain size a farm is not economical and can destroy the fabric of the rural way of life, of the villages and towns.
My other concern is that so much land is being taken out of agricultural production and being paved over for industry, for roads or for hydro lines. Statistics given by the GATT-Fly magazine show that in 1951 Canada had some 70.4 million hectares of farm land and in 1971 the figure had dropped to
67.2	million hectares. By 1976 it had dropped by about another million hectares.
We also see the greater concentration of farm holdings in fewer hands. In 1951 there were 623,000 farms in this country. In 1971 there were only 366,000 farms. I am sure the same trend will show up in the 1981 census which has just been completed.
As a member from rural Canada, I want to make it clear that I am very concerned about the increasing size of farms. The owners of large farms are buying up the small ones and thus becoming larger and larger themselves. The small towns, the rural communities and villages are shrinking. As the farming population shrinks, the need for the small towns is less. In Colorado there are a few farms of township size run by large agricultural corporations. 1 do not want to see that in Canada-agriculture becoming as General Motors is to automobiles. That can be prevented with a rational and sane national agricultural program.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the export development corporation that will be established by this legislation can be part of that program. The corporation can sell our farm products to other countries. It can sell farm products that are more labour-intensive than capital-intensive. It can sell more and more of the specialty crops that can be grown in this country. I think we can do it and compete with the best of countries in the world. On the domestic front, we must become more and more self-reliant so that we can feed ourselves and produce in Ontario, British Columbia and other parts of Canada much of the food we consume. We must move in that
direction. We can only do it by planning and involving the farmers and producers themselves.
My last recommendation is that the export corporation must be controlled by those individuals involved in the agricultural industry itself. Farmers, producers and workers in the agricultural industry must have input as to who will sit on the board of directors. Because of the fact that agriculture is a shared jurisdiction under the Constitution, federal and provincial, and because of the fact that there are literally dozens of provincial marketing boards selling products every day in the world, the provinces as well as the federal government must be represented on the board of directors.
I should like to refer to a relevant example in my province. It is not a food, it is an agricultural product. The province of Saskatchewan provides 35 per cent of the world's potash which is used as a fertilizer and sold to many countries. It is important to have provincial governments involved because of realities such as this, so that there is a co-ordination of food sales, agricultural product sales and such things as potash sales in various countries around the world. I think it is a good idea. I think its time has come. But let us not destroy the idea by an insensitivity to the reality of food and agriculture in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is significant, and I hope farmers across Canada and especially those in my riding will appreciate this, that the first two bills the government is tabling in 1982 in the House of Commons are concerned with agriculture. In recent years we have often had the impression that agriculture is being overlooked. Now that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has tabled a bill whose purpose is to establish an agency for promoting export markets for Canadian producers, I should like to point out that this government, and other Liberal governments that preceded it during the past 15 years, have had a special concern for agriculture as one of our vital sectors. I may add that the fact that the first two bills on which we shall be voting at the beginning of this year in the House concern those Canadians who feed us and are feeding an increasingly large part of the world, demonstrates that a country that is capable of feeding itself and feeding other people besides is also capable of developing its resources and giving its people a healthy environment in which to live.
In the past, when the government set up marketing boards, it was attacked by groups in our society who claimed prices and markets were being supported artificially, and that if the market were free, prices would come down. Before discussing the bill on the agenda today, I want to point out that such claims are entirely false. Prices of farm products have not increased as fast as prices for other commodities. Just compare what you were paying for a quart of milk a few years ago and what you are paying today for a package of cigarettes or a car, neither of which are produced under a quota system, and you
January 29, 1982

will see that the prices of the latter have increased far more. Mr. Speaker, I also wish to congratulate our farmers and prove the extent to which they have been leaders in our society, leaders whose example, unfortunately, we have not always followed. The problem today is essentially one of productivity. Today's high interest rates and inflation are due to the fact that we are still producing at the same rate with the same number of workers, the same machines and the same plants as we were ten years ago, but our production costs are constantly increasing. In the agricultural sector this has not been the case. Western farmers are now producing twice as much as they were ten years ago on the same amount of land. Quebec farmers are getting twice as much milk from the same cow as they did ten years ago. The way these people have been fighting inflation is absolutely marvellous. They have shown what the whole country could be like if we had modernized operations at all levels and had increased our production per capita.
A few minutes ago, I heard the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) say that there were fewer and fewer farmers and that less land was being farmed. With an increasingly small number of farmers and less and less land, Mr. Speaker, we are producing much more than we used to. That is what is called an increase in productivity, that is what is called fighting against inflation, that is what is called fighting against high interest rates. That is how our society must develop. How have we achieved this? 1 have no hesitation in saying that it is quite simply thanks to the Government of Canada. I know that when something goes wrong, Quebecers often lay the blame on the federal government. I cannot say that we owe everything to the federal government; however, I know that the fat Quebec Minister of Agriculture would never say that it is a little because of the federal government. For my part, I shall show you that everything which happens is partly due to the federal government.
Around 1965, under the leadership of the right hon. Lester B. Pearson, if I may quote as an example, the farmers in eastern Quebec and my constituency whom I know quite well, these farmers had tremendous problems because of a lack of financial options for capitalization, of old and outmoded facilities, of production problems, and of people who were not professionals and who belonged to an era when the farmer lived off the land and fed the people around him and then went looking for part-time work to purchase what he could not produce on the farm. Thanks to the farmers who pulled themselves up by their own bootstraps, and thanks also to the assistance provided by the Government of Canada to establish well-developed and well-designed structures, we were able to transform these people into real professionals. How did we achieve this? First of all, by guaranteeing their revenue, by setting production quotas and by establishing marketing boards so that these people could go to the banks and tell them; "We want to borrow; we must replace our equipment;
Canagrex Act
we must update our facilities to be more productive in the future."
Programs were set up. Our farmers obtained loans and invested their shirt in their business. They worked very hard seven days a week. What is the result today? If you go all over a province such as Quebec, you will see new facilities, dynamic producers, hard-working people who have the potential to develop and, most important, who are professionals. Now the farmers are able to do their own accounting, they can make projections for the future and they can do their own financial planning. Mr. Speaker, you know that this is very important because the first duty of the country is to its citizens, and I emphasize this fact because we must understand that whatever party is in power, the main thing in this House has always been that Canada must work for Canadians. In this assembly, in this House of Commons, we have never asked Canadians to give everything for their country because we are all aware of the fact that Canada exists because Canadians wanted it to exist for their own welfare and development.
In this context, I believe that our first duty is to see to it that Canadians can feed themselves. As a Canadian, I am proud today to be able to rise in this assembly and to say that in addition to feeding ourselves, we also feed a large part of the world. We can look at other countries, especially those of the east bloc, with millions of farm workers and an extremely planned economy, which is supposedly communist and is designed to make life easier for the workers, but which are unable to feed their own people. Vast countries like Russia now realize that they are facing an economic disaster because they have stifled initiative.
There is no will to produce more on the same small piece of land, with the same facilities and the same livestock. It is up to us to help them to survive, and I am aware of it. However, 1 would not want Canada to allow these countries to take the money that they would normally use to feed their people to manufacture arms or to build up enormous armies, as we have seen them do in the past. We have come to the point where marketing boards have been established, and we are now on the point of developing the last structures we need, namely, in the pork and the beef industries, where our producers are now facing tremendous difficulties.
We have a few programs to support them but beyond that I think that Canada has demonstrated that agriculture and stability undoubtedly go hand in hand, and I say to those who hope to save five cents per pound of meat by leading farmers to a dead end of instability, not knowing what price they will get to feed themselves and what products they will sell, that the main thing is to know that we can look after the needs of our children and this will happen when production is stabilized and well established. We therefore still have to establish a few marketing boards and we are working at it.

January 29, 1982
Canagrex Act
We have now reached a stage of agricultural development which requires us to look forward. Canada has shown that as a basic structure, as a country which I consider the finest in the world, it is in a position to help the Third World and to feed more than 26 million people, and I believe it. For that purpose, Canagrex, as a new government organization, will help to ascertain the needs of other countries and the products that we can provide and that can be consumed by people living in other climates. In those circumstances, the market is extensive.
It is useless to mention the millions of Canadians who holiday abroad each year. The Caribbean countries mentioned yesterday attract 400,000 visitors, to say nothing of Mexico, Florida and Europe. Tourists are often unable to find in those countries the food they usually eat. This can become a problem. Those countries are surely interested in welcoming wholeheartedly Canadians who spend billions of dollars abroad. That area represents fantastic potential markets for our agricultural products. It is up to us to seize that opportunity. I am pleased to see today that the minister has introduced a bill establishing the organization responsible for gaining access to those markets. Moreover, there are many countries, as I said earlier, which are not self-sufficient in agriculture. Of course, I am aware that we will always have to import bananas or coffee. We will never be in a position to grow all the foodstuffs we need, but we can export a great number of products.
With regard to meat or even to a typical product of my region, blueberries, is a unique product with a fantastic flavour that is now being massively exported to the United States but is still unknown to several countries because our markets have not been extended. Tons of that product remain each year in the fields and woods in my region. They are not picked due to the lack of markets. This is a prospect which could be developed and new markets could be sought. However, the main thing is that with the structures we have set up, our agri-food co-operatives can develop, and our companies with a huge output but not operating at full capacity can find the markets required to dispose of their products.
You know, a turnover of some $42 billion is forecast for the agri-food industry by 1985. That is quite an amount of money. 1 am convinced that the establishment of Canagrex will generate much more than these $42 billion if we combine our efforts and join forces as a nation to develop new markets for the sale of constantly renewable products for daily consumption, especially if we can export the very good name which Canada has earned for itself among our local merchants as a producer of good quality foodstuffs. When you see the Canadian seal of approval of the Canadian government on meat or other foodstuffs, it means that quality is there. We could export this quality. I need not tell you that new markets will continue to open in different parts of the world, for mankind will always need to be fed. That is a basic need. It is clear that the Canadian government cannot afford to develop all these
new markets entirely by itself. It will require, for instance, the co-operation of the provinces.
I am not worried, because we already can rely on the co-operation of farmers. I want to congratulate them once more, because they have become excellent businessmen, and extremely productive ones at that, in just a few years. They have constantly asked the government to give them a break, so that they could fulfill their duties as farmers and feed the Canadian people. No, I am not worried about them. On the other hand, I am concerned about the provincial governments, and when I refer to provincial governments, 1 mean the Quebec government. Here is an example which is very close to me. In my capacity as a representative of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, I was one of the officials who had to negotiate the deal on agricultural expansion and especially land drainage. You probably know that good farm lands are few in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area where I come from.
People often say that our area is some sort of an island deep in the heart of Quebec with a highway linking it to Quebec City. Keeping that in mind we strive to be as self-sufficient as possible in the agricultural fields where we produce. Unfortunately, when that agreement was signed, millions of dollars were earmarked for the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area to help our farmers drain their land. What has happened in the past two years? I found out about it and this is official. First of all the Quebec government began by telling the farmers that it would no longer pay for the engineering costs to prepare the drainage plans they wanted for their land. On the one hand the government of Quebec was offering them money of which 60 per cent came from the federal government to help them, but on the other it was telling them that it would no longer foot the bill for the preliminary projects it used to pay for, that is the blueprints. Try draining without a plan which shows which way your land will slope, how much and so on! The second beef I have is the fact that last year the Quebec agriculture department decided that the funds allotted for farm drainage in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area would quite simply be transferred to Montreal's plain region.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to leave you with the impression that 1 have something against the plain of Montreal for it happens to be our main source of agricultural products in the province of Quebec. But still that is a far cry from trying to empty regions such as ours where the people work extremely hard in a climate which can be unforgiving; as you know, the growing season in Lac-Saint-Jean is more than a month shorter than in the Montreal area. Why go out of their way not to help a region such as mine? Why take the funds which were supposed to be there? I know that many of my friends in agriculture applied for drainage assistance but they were turned down because of the lack of funds. I fully realized that the funds had been shifted over to the Montreal area. It may be that there are more voters in the Montreal area, I do not
January 29, 1982

know, but at times 1 wonder if the party which claims to be pro-Quebec and which calls itself Parti Quebecois would not rather take us for a ride instead of lending us a hand. I would describe that as a sort of living room nationalism. Now and again I derive some pleasure when I describe them as pseudonationalists. All in all, that is a polite way of saying that they are not fascists, but semi-fascists of the extreme right whose sole intent is to sell a flag, to sell a so-called country about which they do not know anything and have no idea whatsoever how it is to be made up.
When you represent a riding and you fight to try to obtain some benefits for those people and then find yourself confronted by a government elected by the same people, a government which instead of working hand in hand with you makes every effort to win votes in a referendum-or a "Renerendum", call it whatever you like-I wonder what the future has in store for our farmers in Quebec, what can our co-operatives expect and what will happen to our agricultural food industry. If it were only up to us here and our policies I would say we have a very bright future. That government holds a majority in the National Assembly and at times it does everything it can to channel away from the Lac-Saint-Jean farmers the funds which end up in other regions; as a result those same farmers might have to pick up the tab, not to mention the fact that they feed the people and that thousands of related jobs are created in the agricultural food industry. I believe that over the years the Government of Canada, the Liberal Party of which 1 am proud to be a member-the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) seems to be smiling. I regard his smile as a sign of approval because in this country, when agriculture is being discussed, even the opposition has good reasons to smile, since agriculture is the industry which has progressed the most in Canada in the last 20 years, under a Liberal government.
Coming back to what 1 was saying, Mr. Speaker, over the last 20 years, the Government of Canada has done well in the field of agriculture and it will continue to do so, not to sell Canada to Quebec farmers but to help a vital sector of our society, namely, our agricultural producers, develop, and increase their output so that they may become the breadbasket of that long-suffering and ill-treated part of the world, the Third World. May I add, Mr. Speaker, that on the other hand, in the last five years, we have seen people in Quebec, going about the province, professing to be nationalists, claiming to be ministers and to be working for their fellow-citizens, who never for one moment understood that they were elected members expressly to represent the people. In Quebec we now have to contend with a group of demagogues who resort to all possible means in an effort to convince people that the federal government is a monster, that Canada is in dire straits and that their future lies in withdrawing within themselves.
Canagrex Act
How is it then that in 1982, 74 of us sitting here to represent six million Quebecers, should decide that the time has come to set up a corporation known as Canagrex, open up our markets the world over, broaden our horizons worldwide, while in Quebec, big Garon goes around saying that they will close down the boundaries, stop importing food products, and communicating with the Canadian government, and break off relations with outsiders? Who is being truthful, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext: That is the big problem!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
I can well imagine Mr. Garon and his tremendous potential at work in 1882, at a time when there were no planes, no telecommunications, no telephones, nothing. Then he could reasonably have claimed the right to be the cock of the walk, because he could not go far in less than two weeks even if it meant only going to his neighbour's place. But fancy that heap of lard coming today in 1982 to advocate the isolation of Quebec! What would he have Quebecers believe?
1 shall never forget what my father told me: Son, beware of him who shows you a gold coin, he is after your dollars. While you are looking at his gold coin, he will rob you of something. Beware. That is exactly what is going on in Quebec at this time. Those people who are promising Quebecers the moon, whether it be in the field of agriculture or any other are also unable to provide for their daily needs. The moon I do not promise, I know I could never get it. I do not pretend to be any brighter than the people who came before me. But the basic commodities that my constituents need from day to day, that I promise on my life, on my conscience to get for them because I know I sit in an assembly where, regardless of party affiliation, people have been worthy enough not to blame the decisions of our forefathers, but to build on what has been left by our predecessors. This is what we are trying to do here.
I am pleased today, Mr. Speaker, as the member for Lac-Saint-Jean, to publicly condemn the Parti Quebecois, its premier and ministers. Our farmers tell us they are faced with a major interest rate problem, they are faced in Quebec with an internal war among pork producers. We are prepared to introduce a share-cost program for pork but meat packers oppose it and some producers as well. While Quebecers are faced with that kind of problem, what is the Parti Quebecois doing, Mr. Speaker? All they could find is a "Renerendum" to find out whether they are separatists or not.
How long can they go on laughing at Quebecers? Those people were elected by more than two million Quebecers but their major concern is not the welfare of their pork producers, it is whether they will be separatists or not, whether we are going to associate or not. Let us wait and see. Time will tell this is nothing but outrageous politicking. What I find most displeasing is that they stuff the minds of our Quebec people and some of our young people with taboos. Stay clear of people who are not like us! Do not speak to anglophones, it is dangerous! Do not go outside the province for work, it is

January 29, 1982
Canagrex Act
dangerous! Let us make us a small country just for ourselves! We, Premier Levesque and his ministers, are going to send ambassadors to talk to people in Ottawa-not Members of Parliament that are elected by the people and are accountable. Careful there, they will trick you! That famous taboo! I discovered something astonishing, Mr. Speaker. It would seem that taboos are an invention of the elite to ensure their control over people. This is what saddens me most, because in my view-I know 1 went somewhat beyond agriculture and 1 apologize to my colleagues, but in Quebec, as soon as we deal with agriculture or any other issue, when we are honest with our constituents we know that being Canadians means a lot, but when people suggest the opposite, it is our duty to prove to our constituents that those people are wrong.
As I said, what is most astounding is to see that elite now trying, under the cover of a fleur de lys, under a flag, under the term Quebecois which by the way they have stolen because some years ago that word described every Quebecer. Now, in their view I am a bad Quebecer. It has even been suggested I am a traitor, because I spend nearly 90 hours a week working for the people who elected me. In my view, to be a nationalist means more than to boast of speaking French, of being a Quebecer. To be a nationalist is a frame of mind. Being a nationalist is living and working every day for the people one represents. To be nationalist is to do your duty. We have seen enough big mouths in Quebec! Stage people, historians, intellectuals, all those members of an intellectual elite, unable to bring the least thing to the population, who can only criticize others, who can only claim to be nationalists, but who are in fact more fascist than nationalist. We have had enough of them in Quebec! We do not need any more of them! In 1982, Mr. Speaker, the moment of truth has come. In Quebec, we now have to build for the future. Let me look at what is going on at this time. The James Bay project is nearly completed, Mr. Speaker. What has the PQ government done in five years? The James Bay project? It is nearly completed and there is nothing else for hydroelectricity. People have been talking about the Ashuapmuchuan for eight years in my region. Studies are still going on to determine if the landlocked salmon will still run the river if they build a dam. They have been studying the salmon behaviour for four years. If you look at other fields of endeavour, you will find that there are still two projects under way in my area: the federal taxation data centre in Jonquiere and the Canada Games gymnasium in Chicoutimi. Nothing else is under way.
And when we go back to basics, this is what it means to be a nationalist. It means coming here to represent the 60,000 people who have elected you, to give them the best, to help them develop not in a closed environment, but at the same rate as all other Canadians. Because you speak French, you have to be a Quebecer and you will no longer speak to anyone else; I will tell you what to do. We have to be open to the world, to develop, to speak as many languages as possible, to be the best
we can, the most developed in every respect, to have a future in every area. That is my duty. From now on, I have decided no longer to tolerate those who will prevent me from doing my job; I have decided to condemn them on behalf of those who have elected me, and if my constituents decide in two years that I have not done my job, they will tell me so in the most democratic way possible, in the way which is the most generally accepted by all.
Personally, I have done my duty. I did not come here to do the pseudonationalists a favour by saying: Yes, I am a Quebecer and I love Mr. Levesque and I love the flag. No, I came here as a real Quebecer. I did not come here to say that I am a Quebecer and I speak French. I came here to get results for my constituents. I came here to help them get ahead, to think for themselves and to show leadership in our country and in the world. I came here to help them increase their output and solve any problems they might have involving production, employment and their health situation-you know, in Quebec we have reached the point where health care just isn't there. Mr. Speaker, during the winter the roads are hardly plowed anymore! Talk about problems! I feel that as a Member of Parliament my work is not much different from anybody else's. When a carpenter goes to work he takes a hammer and nails and the skills he has learned and starts building. I want to do much the same thing. I talk to my constituents. I come here to represent them, to build and work with them, and 1 tell them they should be Canadians, period. I am not trying to shove the Maple Leaf down their throats. I realize they live in a political context called Canada and in another political context called North America. Mr. Speaker, I cannot tolerate-and this also applies to the agricultural sector we are discussing today-seeing people who get themselves elected and, instead of listening to their constituents, grab a microphone and tell them that they have to be Quebecers, they have to be separatists, they have to be in favour of sovereignty or secession, and they have to watch out for the federal government. The latest news is that Quebec is considering a bill-and I am not afraid to say it-to prevent any initiatives by the federal government in the regions. I suppose that the Quebec government-we could compare the matter of the farm drainage agreement-is considering the possibility of letting the federal government invest only in Montreal and Quebec City to keep the people happy and get their votes, and let the people in the "sticks", as Mr. Bernard Landry would say, fend for themselves. This had better not happen, because they will realize that even if they want to separate, federal Members of Parliament are still there. Sooner or later they will have to realize that we are still there and that we mean to serve our constituents.
If I feel, even though it is not in an area of federal jurisdiction, that the Quebec government is preventing me from doing my job or preventing the Government of Canada
January 29, 1982

from spending money in my own riding, like the $800,000 earmarked for Mont Valin or the $40 million earmarked to develop Saguenay Park, something it cannot do because the Quebec government refuses to transfer the land unlike what happened in Shawinigan, I am going to fight to the limit, because I was sent here in the first place to obtain money from the federal government to invest in my own riding and help it develop, and 1 know that in this respect I can count on the understanding of my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative Party and New Democratic Party, because these people have come to realize, as 1 said, that what happened in the past is not perfect, but that it is at least honourable. Those who cannot respect the past, Mr. Speaker, like those in Quebec, cannot respect the present or the future, and any idea runs counter to despotism, something which is not entirely foreign to the Quebec situation just now. Not many ideas from other sources than the Quebec government can prevail at this time. Everything must come from high above, 1 swear, to be worth anything.
But to come back to agriculture, I am proud to be a Liberal and to be part of a government which is made up of 30 Liberal ministers under the leadership of Pierre Elliott Trudeau, forthe Liberal Party has provided Canadian farmers over the years with the tools they needed to really develop. I continue to be proud of that, even when the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville (Mr. Nystrom) says that it is not true. I have been trying to make him understand that everything was not fine and dandy 20 years ago in his own province, and that the Liberal Party has been in power for the past 20 years, except for eight or nine months. The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) may correct me if I am wrong.

The fact remains that everything is selling well just now in the riding and the province of the hon. member. And all is fine, it is one of the healthy provinces in Canada.
1 am sure that the hon. member, if he did not already belong to the No Decision Party, or the New Democratic Party if you prefer, would have been pleased to cross over to this side. Because it often happens that our western friends from the New Democratic Party look much more like converted Liberals than anything else. Sometimes a few of them take on a communistic look, but very soon everything goes back to normal. 1 hope, in that context, if one day you from the New Democratic Party want to join us, that the Chair will let us know. We will show you how to be good Liberals. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, I should address the Chair. At any rate, as 1 said, I am proud to be part of that Liberal Party of Canada.
Often we are asked by young people in our ridings what it means to be a Liberal. Indeed, they are being told that being a PQ is being a Quebecer. A Liberal, what is that? That is something else. They tell us: "How can we be Quebecers and Liberals at the same time? Of course if we are Canadians, we
Canagrex Act
are in the Liberal Party". I said no! This needs not be so. Being a Liberal is first and foremost to be working for the development of the individual person. This is what it means to be a Liberal. We should create a situation in which each and every Canadian can enjoy maximum freedom, whether he be a farmer, a New Democratic Party member, a wavering opposition leader, or a provincial premier. To be a Liberal is to work so that the individual can develop. To be a Liberal does not mean to fight for a province called Quebec, or a country called Canada, to fight for NATO or the Warsaw Pact. To be a Liberal is first and foremost to be an elected representative, a person whose leitmotiv, whose supreme will is to provide opportunities for development and progress for all Canadians. In such a situation, anything can be justified. If the development of individual Canadians is to be achieved through socialization, the Liberal Party can turn socialistic. If the development of individual Canadians is to be achieved through a turn to the right through a strenghtening in the industry, the Liberal Party can move to the right. If in order to promote our development the Liberal Party thinks we have to be communistic, we shall be communistic. This is what it is all about to be a Liberal. To be a Liberal is to be open to all ideas.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) left the Progressive Conservative Party yesterday. Because I know him personally, I can say that he is a great humanist. I have seen him at work in committee, I have discussed with him, and I can even tell you that he is a true member of the Progressive Conservative Party, knowing that he is one of the founders of that party in Alberta, where they are now in power. He has devoted many hours, even in very difficult times and he succeeded in being elected at the very beginning, when there was not a single Conservative in that province. He is a great humanist. What I regret most today, Mr. Speaker, is that, being on this side of the House, I am aware of the situation. However, I feel that on his side there are not enough people who are aware of that. You know, there comes a time, in a politician's life when it is extremely difficult to be left on one's own, when it is so very easy to adopt a party line. But when you are a great humanist, when you think first about the future, about your children, when you think first about the people you represent, you have to promote, for example, the development of farmers. This is one thing. I should have liked the Progressive Conservative Party to understand, for instance, that the development of Canagrex may have depended on the presence of the hon. member for Edmonton East among them. They did not understand and they shouted him down.
The Liberal Party, however, understood that the development of farmers depends on exports, now that we have built a sound agricultural structure in Canada. He has also understood that some people may have different ideas. If we had talked about establishing Canagrex a few years ago, Mr. Speaker, they would have thrown tomatoes at us. It does not

January 29, 1982
Canagrex Act
make sense. Let us develop first our own agriculture, we shall see afterwards whether we should import and export. Let us feed ourselves first! But there were people who believed in it and with whom everyone failed to agree. They were left alone, they were not opposed to, and were told: "Go ahead, do it! Put forward your arguments! That is what it means to be a Liberal!" 1 am proud to be a Liberal, as proud as Canadians were at the last election. I am more and more convinced that they will not change their mind in the next election, especially when people from the New Democratic Party seem to be more concerned about what a country like El Salvador is exporting than about our own exports. I am all too convinced that those who, today, are thrilled with the thought that Liberals are dead and gone in western Canada will soon realize that people will see that being a Liberal is much more than supporting a political party. It is first and foremost to be free to think.
Once again, I congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for this measure and want to remind the farmers of my riding of Lac-Saint-Jean that the first two bills to be introduced in 1982 deal with agriculture, that we start the year working for them, for their development, for the development of their markets and that we shall do the same throughout the year. We are a bunch of Members of Parliament who work for the wellbeing of the farming community. We have introduced special programs for them and we have overcome some difficulties on their behalf and shall continue to do so.
As regards the success of Canagrex, 1 have no doubt whatsoever. The only request I want to make to the minister, and to those who are involved in Canagrex as a corporation, is to show plenty of aggressiveness. And on that point, I shall ask for the support of the provinces, as well as that of the opposition parties: Gentlemen, let us not build Canagrex while planning to destroy it tomorrow morning. Let us build it with the intention of helping its development. Let us take a pile of Canagrex business cards along with us whenever we travel abroad and give them to the people we meet. Let us be ambassadors for Canagrex everywhere we go. Let us not waste time looking for difficulties, something the provinces should also avoid doing. To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I thank you and hope heartily that Canada, under the leadership of Pierre Trudeau and his cabinet, will continue to be one of the world leaders in the area of agriculture and that tomorrow we shall be feeding those who, today, are going hungry in the rest of the world.
