speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a pleasure to rise to speak on this bill which affects ridings such as mine, Huron-Bruce. It is a major producer of many commodities currently being exported and many others that could be exported. Any help given to promote Canadian agricultural products will be of benefit to my riding and many
others. The overflow effects of exports of agricultural products is of help to our secondary industries.
I am pleased to participate in this debate at long last because the export of agricultural product has concerned me throughout my career as a farmer, particularly in the past few years as a participant in a provincial marketing board that aggressively sought markets around the world for our products. Since being elected to this House, I also sat on the special committee formed to examine the usefulness of setting up a national trading corporation to promote general trade under the umbrella of a state trading corporation.
With this background I have been eager to examine the bill which was promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as long ago as May, 1979. I am glad that after three years it has finally come to the point of debate.
As one of the members of the Special Committee on a National Trading Corporation who opposed the majority report recommending a general state trading corporation, I want to make clear my position in relation to the bill now before us. When 1 opposed the majority on the special committee that recommended to this House that we proceed with legislation to create a state trading corporation, I made it clear that I did so for particular reasons.
To quote from the press release which I and my colleague from Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) issued after the report of the special committee was tabled last June, that recommendation to form a state trading corporation flies in the face of advice received both from Canada's private sector businesses and from the many government departments and agencies which appeared before the committee. Bear in mind that this House created that special committee to examine on behalf of the whole House the views of Canadians whose business is to concern themselves with our export trade.
We spent a year conducting hearings here in Ottawa and across the country to hear the views of the Canadian private and public sectors. We also travelled to Europe to examine the experience of a range of European countries which have tried a wide variety of methods of promoting and improving their export performance.
What we found in the course of that full year of study was that the great bulk of informed opinion among Canada's manufacturers and exporters, and indeed the majority opinion among our own public sector experts, was that a state trading corporation was not what was needed to improve our export performance over all. Instead, we received a great deal of expert advice which had never been gathered before in Canada and which should serve as a primer to anyone interested in the matter of Canada's export performance. This advice is all to be found in the transcripts of the committee hearings. I hope it will be researched and used by future task forces and groups concerned with Canada's export performance.
We have heard talk of Canagrex for quite a long time. We did not have the opportunity of examining the bill until very recently. In Ontario there are approximately 26 or 28 marketing boards which are producer-run. A general type of meeting
January 29, 1982

was held with some of those boards. They had an opportunity to express some of their views and concerns but have not had a real opportunity to examine the bill, even the opportunity that we have at this time. I hope that at the committee stage some of these marketing agencies will have the opportunity to examine and look at this board and give their final views before we continue with this agency.
A lot of our marketing boards in Ontario have been very successful in their export endeavours. I was involved in a marketing board. It created a fantastic market for a lot of producers in Ontario. In ten years it completely reversed a trend of 80 per cent domestic use of a product and a 20 per cent export, to an 80 per cent export and 20 per cent domestic use without any sacrifice of consumption of that product in Canada. That is only one board. There are other boards just as successful.
1 know these boards have some serious questions about this proposed agency. Is it going to complement what they are doing or compete with what they are doing? Also, will it compete with our food processors which are actively exporting agricultural products? Are we going to be creating a Crown corporation which will be in direct competition with them? We know, because of the wide range of products involved in export marketing, that we cannot have salesmen who will be experts in all areas. We know that it takes a great amount of market research, and it is my hope that if Canagrex is established it will make use of research and involvement that many of our marketing boards have used up to this time in marketing research that has already been done. If this board is established, I hope the expertise of those people involved in marketing organizations will be utilized and that they will have a place on the board of Canagrex.
It is obvious that there should be people involved who initially have something to sell, people who have the authority to finalize deals and complete the entire package. The agency should have qualified people in all areas, from financing to shipping. As a corporation, Canagrex should be expected to guarantee the high quality of agricultural products for which Canada is held in high regard throughout the world. We want to maintain that.
If this corporation is established, it should start small and not be in competition with services now available either through the federal government or provincial governments. We do not want it to be in competition with a producer or organization directly involved in the export of agricultural products at this time.
Before I continue with the text of my speech, I should like to quote for the record a letter which was sent to me by a constituent. It says:
Re: Further comments requested in your fellow farmers beef questionnaire
The main problems in the farming business today, are inflation and high interest rates.
Canagrex Act
Government dabbling in the "Rob Peter to pay Paul" business, e.g. government loans and grants to Massey-Ferguson and the Chrysler Corporation, etc., etc., and the conferring of special privileges to special groups e.g. the right to strike by public employees, supply management and price-fixing powers to certain farm groups, etc. etc., in the short run look attractive, but in the long pull are disastrous.
You are currently seeking approximately $60 million from Canadian taxpayers to Finance Canagrex, a government export agency whose announced purpose would be to expand agricultural export sales, and so provide jobs for Canadians and earn much-needed balance of payment dollars.
I would strongly support an export sales thrust, but at the same time you are advocating supply management with its accompanying tariffs and trade barriers.
I have a question for you. How many export dollar sales have been earned by products produced under supply-management programs when the same price was charged for export as was paid by our Canadian consumers?
May I suggest that you and your government cohorts concentrate your efforts on balancing the national budget and provide the most humane services possible within that content and leave beef farmers and Canadian citizens generally to get on with the same job in their chosen enterprises?
Enclosed find articles I have clipped from the public press that you may find of interest.
Thanking you for requesting my comments.
The letter is signed by Ross S. Proctor.
The work of the Special Committee on the National Trading Corporation, of which I was a member, had to do with exporting from the enormous Canadian lumber industry to the communications industry and the tool manufacturing industry, from the newsprint industry to the shipbuilding industry and the engineering sector, which exports no hard goods but which exports Canadian expertise in dam building, irrigation projects, oil drilling and so on. The point which we made in opposing the creation of a state trading corporation was that after seeking a very wide range of expert advice, the committee as a creature of this House had an obligation to reflect the advice which it had received when it reported to the House. I maintained then, and still maintain, that the majority on that special committee failed to discharge its primary duty to the House by submitting recommendations to the House in the final report, which did not reflect the advice we had received.
We face an entirely different situation with the bill which is now before us. The creation of an agricultural export corporation has been talked about in Canada for many years now. The present government has campaigned on the promise of creating such a corporation twice in the past five years. In view of the fact that the government has had the introduction of this legislation in mind for so long, it is fair to wonder why it has dragged its feet for so long before introducing the legislation. It is almost two full years since the present government was elected and since the promise to bring in this legislation was formally made in the Speech from the Throne which began this session. The agriculture minister's advisers told the press in May of 1980 that it was only a matter of a few months before the legislation would be presented. One of them was quoted in the agricultural press as saying that the creation of the Canadian agricultural export corporation was "about as high as something can get" on the minister's list of priorities.
Well, farmers now understand sadly and clearly just how fast they can expect results when something becomes a matter of priority with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). It

January 29, 1982
Canagrex Act
took him a year and a half, plus the ammunition of a 70 per cent increase in farm bankruptcies, merely to convince the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to include farmers in the provision of the Small Business Development Bond. Even then he failed. Instead, farmers were allowed limited and restricted access to a small business survival bond, which they could only use when they had become so financially shaky that the banks would no longer want to lend to them. So much for the usefulness of having any matter high up on the list of the minister's priorities.
In fact, I recall when the Minister of Agriculture appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture in the fall of 1980 and told us Canagrex could increase agricultural exports by as much as $3 billion during its first year of operation. One of his officials from the marketing and economics branch of Agriculture Canada announced at that time that there would definitely be money for Canagrex in the 1981-82 budget. By this logic, plus the added assurance that Canagrex would begin very quickly with an aggressive sales campaign, we should by now have been able to look back on a full year of Canagrex operations and, if the minister is to be believed, should be able to take satisfaction in the fact that Canadian food producers have $3 billion more cash in hand to meet the crisis they are facing in farm financing than they in fact have.
However, we cannot look back on a year of Canagrex. Canada's food producers have had to look back on the worst financial squeeze most of them have faced in their whole farming careers or that Canadian agriculture has faced since the Depression of the 1930s. Instead, those producers who have been watching a lifetime's equity melting away month by month during this past year and have watched the outrageous growth of interest rates, have not had the benefit of a single penny of the $3 billion which the Minister of Agriculture said Canagrex could add to the agricultural export drive in its first year alone. Therefore I, along with many other food producers in Canada, am left wondering whether the Minister of Agriculture or his cabinet overlords have the slightest idea what they are talking about when they talk about the value of an agricultural export trading corporation.
I am not for a moment suggesting that Canagrex is a bad idea. I am simply suggesting that if the Minister of Agriculture believes what he says about the value of creating such a corporation, then he should hang his head in shame for taking so long to bring forward legislation which, by his account, could have had such an enormously beneficial effect during the past year in which it could have been operating.
In short, I would like to see the minister talk clear sense and take his responsibilities to Canada's agricultural industry seriously. The last thing that we need in the beleaguered food industry is more rhetoric and empty promises. We need a clear policy, serious planning and prompt implementation of programs. What we have had in the case of Canagrex for almost two years now is apparently a bureaucratic fumble, centred in the cabinet, as a directionless government has concentrated its attention on reshuffling the bureaucratic deck instead of
acting to meet the needs of the agricultural economy in this country.
Having said this, let me say that now that we do have the legislation brought forward for examination and debate, I for one am anxious to see it passed to the Standing Committee on Agriculture so it can be examined in detail and commented on by those who will be affected by the creation of such a corporation and whose livelihood is dependent on their being experts in the field not only of food production but of marketing.
There cannot be any significant objection in Canada, and certainly not among food producers, to the goal of increasing our agricultural exports. This is a thoroughly laudable goal in itself. Certainly, however, there are powerful reasons why this country's food producers will want to look very closely at any scheme brought forward by the present government, even when it is sponsored by the Minister of Agriculture, for whom I think the farming community has had much respect in the past. Recent evidence of the incompetence with which the current government has faced the economic problems of Canada certainly does not inspire confidence in the Canadian agricultural community that any measure brought forward is going to be valuable just because this government says it will be valuable.
We in this party will want to look very closely at this legislation in the committee, and we will want to do so soon. Ever since the present government was elected, the Standing Committee on Agriculture of this House has been spinning its wheels and doing almost nothing to serve the interests of the economic sector whose interests it is charged with protecting.
In almost every Speech from the Throne we have heard, whether it be federal or provincial-and I think we could dig out any throne speech over the last number of years-agriculture has been mentioned, and it has always been said that agriculture is the backbone of this great country. However, that apparently seems to be about all that happens. We only get lip service to agriculture when the crunch comes.
Another reason, of course, is that the Minister of Agriculture has not brought any real grist to the mill. There is a vacuum, a powerlessness, in this government which has cost the farming community in Canada unnecessary billions of dollars in outrageous interest charges as a direct result of government economic and fiscal policy. And there is a vacuum where there ought to be a powerful and effective minister of agriculture in the cabinet, where, once upon a time, there was such a minister.
For all these reasons the agricultural sector in Canada will want a full examination of this legislation now before us at the committee stage, even though the need for an improvement in the prospect for Canadian agriculture is immediate.
As a representative of one of Canada's leading pork and beef producing areas, I can tell the House with certainty that there is absolutely no value for our redmeat producers in increasing our markets for pork and beef if we are going to
January 29, 1982

continue to fetch prices below the cost of production. If we increase beef and pork sales by $3 billion a year, under the present price regime Canadian farmers could expect to lose more millions as they subsidize foreign consumers more heavily, the way they now subsidize Canadian consumers. Cana-grex, in other words, is of no help to the agricultural sector in Canada if it merely increases our food exports without increasing the returns to farmers.
So, as we look at this legislation in committee, we will need to be convinced that Canagrex, as it has been envisioned by this government and the bureaucrats who drafted the legislation, will in fact serve the interests of Canada's food producers and not merely fit into some macroeconomic strategy as part of Canada's over-all trade picture or as an aspect of Canadian foreign policy.
On the face of it I believe there are grounds for hoping that Canagrex can work to the advantage of Canada's trade performance over-all and to the benefit of the food-producing sector, which should be the primary beneficiary. But, I add, let us be certain that it does before we come to the final debate in the House on the legislation now before us.
To ensure that Canagrex is workable and does work to the benefit of food producers I support the reference of this legislation to committee promptly for rapid and very careful and close study. I hope, when the committee finishes its examination and reports this bill, it will have proved itself harder working and more competent than the government's lack of interest in agriculture has allowed it to be thus far during the course of the present Parliament.
Canada's food producers have been crying out for clarity and competence in the government's management of agriculture, and they have not yet got it from this government.
I hope we can unite in sending this bill to committee with the strong demand that it receive prompt, close and careful scrutiny and comment from a wide range of groups which will be affected by the creation of an agricultural export trading corporation such as the government has now, at last, proposed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased, at the end of this week, to be able to take part in the debate on the Canagrex bill, especially since this corporation constitutes our challenge to the food industry in the eighties. A few weeks ago, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) tabled a white or beige paper in which he stressed the projected increase in the world population and the enormous markets that would be open to us during the next 20 years. The white paper has three major concerns: development of resources, development of markets and thematic agricultural research. I think the bill now before the House is aimed more specifically at realizing the second objective. It is becoming absolutely essential for Canada to develop export markets, considering the fact that surpluses are a problem for many producers. In my riding, people also have this problem and they have a good understanding of export markets.
According to our statistics and projections, Canada will be able to increase agri-food exports by about 60 per cent during the next twenty years. But how am I to reconcile the words of the previous speaker who said that he is anxious to examine the legislation in committee for the benefit of our farmers, with those of his official critic, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), who said that the Minister of Agriculture could wait, that they had plenty of time, that there was no rush and that the House could debate the bill for a few days more. Honestly, when you consider that farmers have been asking for this legislation for several years! We made a promise during the election, the corporation was mentioned in the throne speech and even the members of the opposition agree with the concept. That is why I fail to understand their desire to delay the democratic process. However, if they are willing to refer the bill immediately to committee, I should be glad to sit down and give them a chance to vote. To most Canadian farmers, international trade opens a host of possibilities and will enable them to expand their business and to get a return on their often quite considerable capital investment.
Many farmers are now producing at 60 per cent, 50 per cent or even 40 per cent of their capacity because of a lack of

January 29, 1982
Canagrex Act
markets for their products. The corporation we are proposing will be a focal point for the entire agri-food sector in Canada, because not only producers but also processors will be interested in meeting the challenge of Canagrex. In fact, the real challenge for Canada in the eighties will be to be able to market processed farm products, thus providing a living wage for many more Canadians and making a very substantial contribution to our balance of payments. In 1980, Canada succeeded in exporting $7.8 billion worth of agricultural products. Unfortunately, the vast majority of these were primary products, involving a minimum amount of labour, which of course had a negative impact on our employment rate. Once Canagrex becomes the instrument of our agricultural export policy, I am convinced that we could easily exceed the $2.7 billion surplus we had in 1980 and probably will have this year. In Canada we must rely on advanced production techniques. We have a large pool of workers and, even more important, we have enough space to increase farm production.
Sales abroad now account for 40 per cent to 45 per cent of the normal income of farmers, and this percentage could increase substantially if Canagrex fulfills its mandate. Feeding the world is a constant challenge. We only have to look at the Third World countries, at the enormous trading potential with the socialist bloc or at the even greater demand from the Arab countries to realize that Canada can easily get a share of these markets with the help of experienced salespeople. This is why I hope that this new corporation will be staffed with qualified people who will probably be able to operate from within our embassies and sell our farm products instead of merely selling equipment. This would be a welcome change for a constituency like Shefford, where there are poultry, egg, maple syrup, apple, pork, dairy and other producers. Maple syrup is a very good example. We now have a surplus of millions of pounds in Canada and this product is not well known in most parts of the world. We have a very limited market of people who know this extraordinary product, but they are just a minority in the world, and I am convinced that with a good sales program we could first sell our surplus, and then increase our production.
Among the problems now facing agriculture, one of the most important is that of pork production. In Quebec, pork production is virtually at a standstill; a number of producers are just about bankrupt and there is a very big surplus. I am convinced that even though our slaughterhouses and our federations have developed markets in Japan and the United States, there are many other opportunities elsewhere in the world, and if Canagrex could not compete with them, but co-operate, our farmers might earn a decent living. According to the most realistic projections, the world population should reach 6.4 billion within the next ten years. Such an increase means a lot of mouths to feed and the challenge facing Canadian producers is great.
I am even more satisfied when I see who the officials of Canagrex will be. This corporation will not turn out to be the
type of institution which suffers from structuralism and is nothing more than a bunch of thinkers. We intend to have a corporation managed by a board made up of 11 directors who will be directly responsible to the Minister of Agriculture, seven of whom will be appointed from outside the federal public service. And with all due respect to our public service, I am convinced that we can find seven Canadians outside our system who can make Canagrex, as well of course as all Canadian farmers, benefit from their knowledge of agriculture, marketing, and the marketplace itself.
There will also be a policy advisory committee which will be made up of representatives from the provincial governments. A while ago, one of my colleagues spoke about problems with the provincial governments, but I am certain that the provincial governments will consider it their duty to take an active part in an organization such as Canagrex because if the balance of payments of Canada is improved by the work of Canagrex, it will be of great benefit to the provincial governments. The corporation will include representatives from business and farm associations who will be in a position to advise the minister in all areas concerning the market development strategy. Management will be restricted. A president and two vice-presidents will be hired to manage Canagrex under the board of directors. I do not think farmers would have liked it if we had created a top-heavy structure that would have hampered their ability to communicate with and understand those who will try to open up new markets. Another significant aspect of the legislation, one which I hope will be found in other bills in the future, is the provision in clause 31 that the corporation will prepare a three-year plan. This means that every Canadian farmer, everyone in the agri-food industry, processors and even bankers will know in advance where Canagrex is going, what its objectives are for the three following years. And I quote:
(2) The corporate plan referred to in subsection (1) shall set forth
(a)	the purposes and general objectives of Canagrex, not inconsistent with this
act or the bylaws of Canagrex; and
(b)	the projected activities of Canagrex in the three financial years covered by

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to enter into debate today. 1 welcome the opportunity to make some comments about the bill before us. Bill C-85 establishes the Canadian Agricultural Export Corporation, Canagrex. Hopefully the corporation will carry out the functions desired by the minister to promote, facilitate and engage in the export of agricultural food products. Also it shows that the government is at least willing to recognize that there is an agricultural industry out there.
Please allow me to refer to a certain amount of concern which I have, Mr. Speaker, about the act, the subject relating to it and the powers given to the corporation. Also allow me to mention other concerns which I should like discussed at great length in committee and debated on the floor of the House. When we were looking at other questions regarding Canagrex to which we must have answers, we looked at such things as the role of Canagrex and the export of agricultural goods. We must ask ourselves whether it will be in support of or in competition with other exporters, both large and small. Who has the power to determine the sale and price of goods once a market is found? Is this the sole responsibility of Canagrex, or will it be shared with other departments such as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce or the Department of
External Affairs? How many fingers are actually in the pot when it comes to who has final say in sales to the corporation? The co-operation among Canagrex, other government departments, organizations, the agricultural community and national marketing boards is of utmost importance. This brings us to the thought of developing a multiple government agency which must relate with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of External Affairs or whatever the new massive complex may be. I would hate to see it evolve into a situation where trade-offs are made of manufactured goods coming in and out of the country, where we must deal with other department agencies and be willing to trade some of our produce to another country provided that we are willing to accept its manufactured goods or possibly even its produce which competes with our own. The actual sales being made as a result of negotiations between countries and departments are of major concern as well as the resulting agreements. As to the question of whether or not Canagrex should be a Crown corporation, it should be examined closely both in committee and here in the House.
I am sure that hon. members are aware of my concerns about Crown corporations, since I am the Post Office critic. We are a little shell-shocked on this side and so are the people in this country when it comes to Crown corporations, especially when we look at the Post Office and Petro-Canada. We on this side of the House together with many people in the agricultural field are leery of Crown corporations.
I feel we have a sufficient number of Crown corporations in Canada now. But whether Canagrex should be a Crown corporation or a wing of the Department of Agriculture or some other department of this government should be weighed in order to determine what is most advantageous to our country and to our farm community.
In this past week the word "partners" has been mentioned. The possibility is that Canagrex would enter into a partnership in sales and negotiations. Farmers in Canada do not want to be partners with the government, assisted yes, but not partners. We have too much government intervention in agriculture now. On page 6 of Bill C-85, we read:
(g) purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and hold real and personal property for actual use by Canagrex-
My concerns about this corporation are increased, having read that particular subclause.
1 am concerned about jobs. Who are the people who will serve on the board of directors of this corporation? Who will be its vice-presidents? Who will go out looking for areas in which to sell our produce? Who will make the contracts? 1 hope these positions will not be patronage positions for those who have done well for the Liberal Party. I hope they will not be political appointments. I have sufficient faith in the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to believe that he will ensure that the best possible personnel will be put into this corporation and they will be agriculturally-related individuals.

Therefore, we must take our opportunity to present our views to the House.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Ferguson), while speaking to this bill earlier this week, said that with Canagrex we must learn to walk before we can run. I agree with the parliamentary secretary. We must walk before we run. That is why we should not "run" this bill through the House. We should "walk" this bill through the House to ensure that it is the best possible bill for agriculture that this House can produce.
Certainly we must increase our agriculture exports in Canada. All members on this side of the House are aware of that. I am sure that all members on that side of the House are aware of that too and agree. We have always been informed and had the idea that Canada had a food trade surplus. We have. But the surplus is dependent directly on the world grain market, world grain trade, and Canada's sale of grains around the world. When we take the grain sales out of the figures, we find that we have an ever-worsening food trade deficit in Canada. That is something we must work together to turn
Canagrex Act
around. While doing this we must also ensure that we protect our own agricultural community from imports of goods that we can grow here in Canada. Such as those grown in my area, which include apples, fresh fruits and vegetables, oil seeds and soybeans.
If we are going to look for markets around the world for our produce, we must also ensure that we protect produce in Canada that can be produced and sold also within our boundaries. It must be protected from imports from abroad. We must promote home sales as well as sales abroad. It is important that agriculture is helped at this time in Canada.
It is very important that we here in Ottawa take steps to help agriculture. We have to help find markets. Assistance must be given in the selling of goods to these markets. We must protect the goods that can be grown competitively here within the country. All sectors in agriculture must be helped. Agriculture has tremendous problems today. There is a tremendous cost-price squeeze placed on the producers in this country. Government tends to forget farmers, all levels of government, be they municipal, federal or whatever. It is very easy to say that farmers make up only a small percentage of the voters in this country and that we must really look to the consumers who make up some 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the voters. We must keep prices down to those consumers to ensure their votes. We must keep the cost of living down. We must keep inflation down. But let us not forget that farmers are also consumers, and on the average they consume much more than other sectors of the population. They too are having problems. They have problems with overhead which is continually rising. But the prices farmers receive for their goods are already on what is classified by too many people in the country as the top rung. These expenses which are continually climbing the ladder will eventually push the farmer off the ladder. The farmer faces tremendously increased costs in the transportation of his goods to the marketplace. The farmer faces increased costs in seed to plant his crops. There are increased costs for animal feed, fertilizer for his fields, labour to work his fields, and a tremendous increase in the cost of energy for his buildings and equipment. In addition, we have seen in the last few years a tremendous increase in the cost of equipment used on the farm.
What do the farmers do about it, Mr. Speaker? They go into debt; they have to in order to survive. They borrow money at the first of the year to put their crops in and hope they have a good year so they can pay it off at the end when they hope they can sell that crop. What do they borrow it at? Their interest rates are at 20 per cent or more. This kind of burden can no longer be placed on agriculture.
I am swamped in my constituency office, as I am sure members on both sides are, by farmers coming in with financial problems. Proud people with a 40-year farm history, people who have paid off as many as five mortgages on their farm to get to the position they are now in. People who have raised proud families, many of the children having returned to

Canagrex Act
agriculture. One particular case comes to mind, Mr. Speaker, of a farmer whose son recently had his farm foreclosed and has himself been given 60-days notice. There are countless examples of this, Mr. Speaker, but this is not the bill on which to debate that.
They have been turned down by lending institutions, be they banks, government agencies or whatever. They do not know which way to turn. We are now debating some method of offering assistance in selling their goods and products. We must also consider the bankruptcies in agriculture. There is talk that the number of farm bankruptcies is much lower than what people believe; they are not really at a critical level. That is a fallacy, Mr. Speaker. I mentioned earlier that farmers are proud people. That is what keeps the bankruptcy figures down. If it reaches that stage in agriculture, you not only lose your home and your farm, but your whole life's work, your pension plan.
What do farmers do in that kind of situation? They borrow money, Mr. Speaker, at those high interest rates on which most of us would turn our backs and do anything but borrow. Or they go outside the farm and get a job at Stelco, Dofasco, Hydro or wherever. Then they come home at night and on the weekends and farm their land in order to keep it and to prevent bankruptcy. Or their wives go back on the labour market instead of staying home and looking after the family. When it comes down to it, rather than declare bankruptcy, most of those farmers will put their farm on the market for what they can get, thereby ensuring payment to their creditors rather than taking the final step into bankruptcy. So the bankruptcy figures, Mr. Speaker, do not represent the problems in agriculture today.
If we are to arrive at the best way to market farm products, we must understand and address the problems of the producers, we must assist marketing not only within Canada but around the world. The Farm Credit Corporation has been given a new lease on life to help the agricultural industry, and the Small Business Development Bond program is going to be given great amounts of money to assist those farmers in dire straits but, typically, it is all too little, too late and masked in confusion.
If a farmer goes to the FCC, he is told the regulations are correct and he must be turned down by banks and other lending institutions before he qualifies. It is not the fault of the FCC's field men, Mr. Speaker. Those who man the offices are capable and very concerned. It is the fault of a government that will not properly fund the corporation to enable its officials to look at the farmers' problems and help them to produce the goods we hope to sell around the world through Canagrex.
So the farmer, having been told that he must be turned down by the banks first, turns to the banks, Mr. Speaker, and inquires about the Small Business Development Bond. What is he told? We do not have the regulations yet from the government as to what it entails. Two months after the budget was brought down the banks still do not know what to do about it.
Now that we see a draft of the Small Business Development Bond program, what do the regulations say? They say you must first be turned down by other lending institutions. So we have the FCC saying you must be turned down by the banks and other lending institutions, and the Small Business Development Bond regulations saying the same thing. Where does the circle end, Mr. Speaker? When is that government over there going to assist farmers with acceptable interest rates?
This government makes promises. Canagrex was one, and a good one, but there were other promises made during the election. Farmers in my riding were told that the government would review the capital gains tax with the idea of reducing or eliminating it for farmers. They were told that V-day would be advanced from 1971 to 1974. What actually took place, Mr. Speaker? The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) took those promises, threw them out the window and hit the farmers harder than they have ever been hit before.

PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should declare a moratorium on metrication, disband the Metric Commission and. refer the question ol conversion to the metric system to a standing committee of the House of Commons for study and review, and that the review extend to all aspects of the metric system and include the hearing and consideration of the views of interested persons and organizations and that the committee make recommendations that appear to the committee then to be necessary or desirable; and that the committee have the power to adjourn from place to place within Canada.
He said: In the Monday, January 11 edition of the Kingston Whig-Standard, there was an editorial entitled "Metric Madness: An Unconscionable Assault on Freedom." I would just like to read, for a moment, the first two or three paragraphs, because I think they are very interesting. The editorial states:
For people who can't tell the difference between an end and a means, I recommend a Mac Tackaberry.
In a front-page story the other day in The Whig-Standard, Mr. Tackaberry said all that there is to say. I'm only writing this to praise him.
For Mr. Tackaberry, there is no difference in principle between metric law and martial law. There isn't.
And for this Kingston businessman, metric measurement itself is not the issue. It isn't.
It is the use of force, by government, to do something that it wants to do, and to make many people do what they do not want to do.
Mr. Tackaberry says that he is prepared to resist the forcible imposition of metric law; that he is prepared to let the government close down his business, with its 30 employees; that he is prepared to go to jail.
How did this all come about? Canada has recognized the metric system since 1871. It was a voluntary system, and I emphasize the word "voluntary". Then, on January 16, 1970, to be exact, a white paper was tabled in the House of Commons. As is customary, the white paper, when it was tabled, was briefly commented on by a representative from each of the parties. At that time, our then House leader, Mr. Ged Baldwin, the then hon. member for Peace River, as recorded at page 2471 of Hansard, had this to say:
1 agree that there must be a continuous and detailed study. We are prepared to co-operate with the government in this regard ... I would strongly urge the minister to give some thought to having the white paper he tabled today
Metrication
submitted either to a special or to a joint committee so that there might be a continuous study and reports from time to time to this committee by the boards the minister proposes to set up.
There was no reference of the white paper to a committee, and there was no debate in the House of the basic principles of metrication. However, based on that white paper, the Metric Commission was set up. I am not sure under which minister it was set up. I assume it was the then minister of industry, trade and commerce. However, the Metric Commission was comprised of four bureaucrats who were out of touch with the real world, the same types of bureaucrats, I would suspect, who prepared the budget which was handed down in the House on November 12.
Once this metrication committee was set up, it proceeded to try to implement metrication in the country. The committee members were able to persuade some of their fellow bureaucrats in the other provinces to go along with them. In Saskatchewan, for example, the land titles act was changed. The basic law of the land in the province of Saskatchewan was changed by an order in council dated April 20, 1976, prepared by bureaucrats and presumably signed by a minister somewhere along the way. However, what was interesting to find out, as we did, was that the matter of changing the land titles system in the province of Saskatchewan and, I assume, in the other provinces as well, was never debated in the legislature. As a matter of fact, when some of the Saskatchewan Members of Parliament found out that this order in council had been passed in Saskatchewan, we contacted some of the provincial MLAs and some of the ministers of that government and we asked, "What has happened? What went on? You have changed the land titles system to metric." What was their response? They said, "You are crazy. We never did that." We said, "Well, here is your order in council."
The Metric Commission bureaucrats persuaded the bureaucrats in Saskatchewan to change the land titles system. It is really a physical impossibility to change the land system from acres to hectares because the land in the prairies is surveyed on the square mile. There are 640 acres to the square mile, and 160 acres to a quarter section. One cannot convert to the metric system without having a whole bunch of decimals, which is absolutely ridiculous. The Metric Commission bureaucrats, as well, persuaded the bureaucrats in the provinces to change our speed limit signs in the provinces to kilometres per hour. There was no discussion and no debate. It was passed by order in council.
It was not until December of 1976, or early in 1977, that the question of the metric system ever arose in the House again, but by then it was a fait accompli. The metric system has moved along to the stage where the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, the Hon. Otto Lang, brought a bill into the House which was to change the Canadian Wheat Board Act, to change the Grain Commission Act, and to change the Weights and Measures Act from imperial to metric, making the imperial system illegal. That led to quite a lengthy debate.

He is not here, either. However, his argument was that the change to metrication would save the farmers and grain producers some $5 million a year. He could not explain it. They were not letting anybody off. They were spending all this money on conversion of their scales, but he said, "We are saving the prairie farm producer $5 million."
I travel throughout my constituency on a regular basis. I visit every elevator in my constituency, and there are a lot of them. In my travels I have only found one elevator agent who agrees with and is in favour of the metric system. He is in favour because he started after the system was imposed. However, without exception when you visit an elevator, the agent will tell you two things. First, they wish it had never been changed. Second, 99 per cent of the farmers delivering grain to the elevator say to the agent that it is fine to receive their ticket marked in tonnes, but they would like to know how many bushels were on their load and how many bushels they have sold.
This not only concerns the elevators but the stores. We have moved to the stage where a recent order in council has made metrication in the stores compulsory. Two years ago when it was rumoured that the stores would be forced to go metric, I visited many storekeepers in smaller towns where there is only one store.
Generally speaking, such a store is run by an elderly couple. They live above the store because their income is marginal. They told me that if they had to convert to metric and spend money on new scales, their income could not stand it and they
would have to close. We would have a situation where there is a small town and no store. That is fine for young people with a car. They can drive to the nearest city or town where there is a store. However, the senior citizens who live in those towns, and there are many of them, will be faced with great difficulty when buying their groceries.
The grocery stores are being forced to convert to metric, and we do not even manufacture such scales in Canada. They must be imported. The cost to convert the scales in Canada will be $584 million, and that is only an estimate. Who will pay for that conversion? It will be added on to the price of the goods and you, I and other consumers will pay the cost. Our cost of living will increase. This is inflationary. No wonder our cost of living keeps going up.
In addition, money is being spent on advertising. We are going to pay Madame Benoit and Bruno Gerussi $110,000 for appearing on a television advertising campaign. They will show how to cook food using the metric system. I do not think it will taste any different, but that is good money for them. I understand that $1.8 million will be spent to advertise the change to metric in the grocery stores. This is unbelievable.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to the motion put forward by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) concerning the metric conversion program.
The motion before us suggests that we should replace an effective and efficiently running organization, namely, the Metric Commission of Canada, with another committee which will not only duplicate much of the work already completed by the commission but which will have no responsibility to achieve any concrete results.
The program that we already have in place is progressing very well and is about to come to a successful conclusion in the near future, largely due to the co-ordinating efforts of Metric Commission Canada.
Metrication
I would like to explain how Metric Commission Canada has already fulfilled and is now fulfilling exactly the role proposed by the hon. member for a standing committee. Since its inception, the commission has assumed the responsibility, and its mandate, of reviewing all aspects of the implementation of the metric system in Canada. From the time that all House leaders supported the white paper on metric conversion in 1970-I would remind hon. members opposite of that- through to the end of 1975 when the investigative phase of the conversion program was essentially completed, the Metric Commission was actively involved in assessing the impact of metric conversion on every sector of the economy in Canada.
I would like to quote from the statement of the former member for Peace River, Mr. Baldwin, made at the time of the tabling of the white paper on metric conversion. He said:
I agree there must be a continuous and detailed study. We are prepared to co-operate with the government in this regard.
That is what Mr. Baldwin, a Conservative member, had to say at that time. Yet, when the Metric Commission has been and continues to be, engaged in assessments and reviews, there is a motion on the floor to undo the work of the commission.
An integral part of carrying out this assessment was and still is the co-operation and support received from over 2,000 volunteers representing private industry, agriculture, education and consumers at large. These representatives were chosen by their peers through national associations and organizations, large and small, to work on sector committees in order to recommend, guide and monitor individual conversion plans which reflect the best interests of their respective industries.
Speaking of the education sector, I was speaking to a teacher from a junior high school who is a friend of mine in Toronto, and a very reasonable person. She was saying that the students of this generation have picked up metric very easily.

subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: So did I. Years ago. Where were you brought up?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is shocking that you want to go back to this. These sector committees continually review the progress of conversion in light of changing conditions such as, for example, consumer reaction, trade opportunities and economic and practical experience. This is an ongoing and knowledgeable review by those who will bear the brunt of the costs and the benefits of metric conversion. This continual review, assessment and corrective action are the ongoing business of sector committees, and their worth is efficiently co-ordinated by Metric Commission Canada.
It should also be emphasized that it has taken many years of co-operative effort to acquire the necessary knowledge and expertise to make the multitude of decisions required to set each industry on the least costly and most judicious course of metric conversion. This has been accomplished through volunteer representatives under the co-ordination of the Metric Commission.
One of the great achievements of Metric Commission Canada has been to organize some 100 sector committees,

January 29, 1982
Metrication
bringing together representatives from large and small businesses alike, from management and labour, to sit down together around one table and to work co-operatively toward a common objective. This accomplishment is not a minor one and it should not be expected that a newly-appointed standing committee could do anything different from what the Metric Commission has already achieved.
As part of its responsibility to co-ordinate metric conversion in Canada, the commission continually monitors the views of Canadians at large and is open to representation by both individuals and organizations.

A further responsibility which has been assigned to Metric Commission Canada is to make available a broad range of information materials both for those who specifically request them and for general use by the public. The co-ordination and dissemination of information is most essential when the implementation of conversion plans are under way. This is one of the key roles of the Commission, and the one which is only just coming to a peak as the implementation phase passes the mid-point of completion. Any disruption in metric conversion will seriously undermine the information program which is progressing not only through Metric Commission Canada but, more important, through the auspices of the various sectors of the Canadian economy as they implement metric conversion.
Another of the key functions of Metric Commission Canada is to make recommendations to the minister regarding the future progress of conversion in Canada. In this regard, the sector committees which have embarked on the metric conversion program, with the guidance and support of the government through Metric Commission Canada, have made it clear that metric conversion cannot be accomplished unilaterally by industries alone and that the government's commitment and
leadership are essential to the successful completion of the program. It does not appear logical for the government to terminate the support and co-ordination provided by Metric Commission Canada just as the program is reaching its final stage. Without the co-operation and involvement of all levels of government, metric conversion is likely to be unnecessarily prolonged and the interests of consumers and businesses will suffer accordingly.

speechtext: Throw it out entirely.

subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is extremely important to recognize the amount of time, effort and money expended by thousands of people across Canada from every walk of life in support of the decision to proceed with metric conversion in an orderly fashion. This decision was taken to ensure that Canada is in step with the rest of the world.

subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE

This effort is about to come to fruition. I cannot help it if hon. members opposite still prefer to live back in the ice age. That is up to them.
The implementation phase which has been under way in some sectors of the economy since 1975 is close to 60 per cent complete at this time. Over 50 per cent in the 94 sectors of the Canadian economy which have published sector plans expect that their programs will be substantially completed before December, 1984. By this time, metric measures will be used by Canadians for most commercial and legal transactions.
Is this really the time to impose a moratorium on metric conversion?

subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, absolutely. You should never have started.

subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
On the contrary, I suggest that this is the time to strengthen our effort, to realize the benefits and to complete the program. Let us not carry on forever analysing the pros and cons of metric conversion. It has been said the most costly aspect of conversion has been the debate. The expenses incurred over the years on debating the pros and cons, the costs and benefits, and the problems and opportunities would likely have paid for the major portion of the conversion program itself. I do not think that we should add to that expense with another protracted debate.
I would like to illustrate how different sectors of the Canadian economy are adapting to the changeover to metric with a minimum of fuss.
Metric conversion in the oil and gas industry is an example of a conversion that has proceeded relatively smoothly. I know that my hon. friend is very interested in the oil and gas industry. That is one example. This has been brought about by the leadership exhibited by the Canadian Petroleum Association. The Association, realizing the necessity to formulate a well-thought-out plan for the industry, established a committee in 1972 with the responsibility of bringing about an orderly transition to metric conversion on a least cost basis. The
January 29, 1982

committee is truly representative of the industry and comprises individuals knowledgeable of all phases of the industry. In this sector, which is very important to Canada, production and field operations have been essentially metric since January, 1979. Similarly, the mining industry and the chemical industry are now operating to a great extent with metric measurements.
Motor vehicle manufacturers are one of the leaders in Canada's metric conversion program. In this regard, Canada had to keep in step with the United States automotive industry which started the move to metric. Early in the conversion process the industry identified many long-term advantages to going metric and, by careful planning, were able to introduce a progressive conversion, thus minimizing the short-term costs. Some of the advantages foreseen were standardization of designs and components, reduction in the number of sizes of items such as fasteners and the use of one system of measurement throughout worldwide operations.
An example of how a major industry has an impact on other supplying sectors is metric conversion in the rubber and plastics industries. With automobiles and parts designed and manufactured in metric terms, many rubber and plastic components have also been converted to metric. Further progress toward metric conversion is expected as more companies are identifying their products in metric terms in response to the market demands. Metric production is also under way in the reinforced plastics composites, injection moulded parts and many other plastic items in response to market demands.
The rubber and plastics industries have both stated that hard conversion, with product size rationalization, will be pursued wherever possible for long-term benefits, with the ultimate objective of international standardization. Conversion is to be compatible with related domestic and worldwide industries and achieved with minimal cost.
Metric conversion in Canada is not confined to heavy industries. There is considerable progress in areas that relate to consumers.
Metric conversion of specific food products has included prepackaged meats, confectionary items, dairy products, canned and frozen fruits and vegetables, jams and jellies, juices, biscuits, cooking and salad oils, sugar and snack foods.
This conversion in the food industry, a sector of the economy that impacts on every consumer in Canada, has been achieved with a minimum of inconvenience. In many cases the consumer is not even aware that the product he or she is buying has been converted to metric.
It is estimated that 75 per cent of prepackaged grocery products have been converted to metric sizes. Grocery manufacturers have completed this planning on a voluntary basis via 16 industry-sector committees. The benefits for the Canadian consumer resulting from metric conversion have been less proliferation of product sizes and ease in calculating unit prices and in comparing product prices because of uniform product sizes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Ostiguy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to display more restraint and moderation than the previous speaker in my attempt to show that the metric conversion process really meets the expectations of Canadians in this new decade. It is a pity the hon. member opposite who spoke before me is still living in the thirties, but I want to tell him that this government is legislating for the young people of the future, not for the past. And I might tell him also that people of my age may have some difficulty adjusting to the new system, but there is no point asking younger people to think in terms of pounds and miles and so on. All they know is the metric system. Therefore, as a responsible government, we have to legislate for the present and mainly for the future, for the generation which will take over from us in a few years.
The motion seeks to stop all metric conversion in Canada and to set up a standing committee to reconsider metric conversion. I think that after ten years, the time to set up a
January 29, 1982

committee to find out where we stand is long past. I notice that newspapers, commercials and supermarkets are already advertising in kilograms and in pounds. Since January, all advertising by the big food chains has been in kilograms and pounds so that people can get used to it. Several sectors with representatives on the Metric Commission have pointed out that in their industries, metrication is almost completed. Until now, various sectors of business, industry, education, labour and agriculture have published 94 conversion plans. Today, 1 rose precisely to speak on behalf of Canadian producers, consumers, etc. Eighty per cent of these sectors are expecting to reach their conversion objective before December 1984. Moreover, the conversion of scales in retail food stores, which is the last major program to affect consumers, is now being implemented in most Canadian cities.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the progress of metric conversion and its importance for the Canadian economy. Here is important news for farmers: the Versatile Manufacturing company, from Winnipeg, which produces agricultural machinery, has just launched on the market a line of farming tractors designed in metric units. Canadian subsidiaries of American corporations, including John Deere, Caterpillar and others, had already done so several years ago. Let's not forget that total Canadian exportations of agricultural products are worth more than $6 billion annually, which represents almost 40 per cent of cash revenues for farmers, and this figure equals our fourth largest field of export to the United States, newsprint. Over 80 per cent of these agricultural products are exported to metric countries.
From now on, newsprint and pulp will be traded at the international level only in metric measures. Heaven knows how important that industry is for us in Canada! The province I have the honour of representing in the House, the province of Quebec, is an important newsprint producer and exporter. The oil and natural gas sectors having been converted to the metric system, almost 50 per cent of our exports, even those destined for the United States will from now on be measured in metric.
Mr. Speaker, let us add to that the ever-increasing share of our exports to the European Economic Community, Japan, Mexico, Brazil, the Soviet Union and China, all countries which converted to the metric system long before we did. It will then be realized how important metrication is. At least two thirds of Canada's $10 billion exports increase in 1980 were shipped to countries other than the United States. It should also be understood that if we want to keep on benefiting from the products we grow or make in Canada, we must export in order to be able to import the products we want.
Since the Canadian government adopted, its metric system policy ten years ago, our exports as well as their percentage expressed in metric units, have increased threefold. Since the beginning of the week, yesterday as well as the day before, we have been discussing Canagrex, a corporation engaged with the export of agricultural products, and if our Canadian
Metrication
exporters and farmers want to trade with the countries I have just mentioned they must go metric. The Task Force on packaging of freight goods recommends and promotes the conversion of standards for palettes, containers and charging units. Ironmonger shops within the iron and steel industry are already metric and the construction industry is proceeding well. Of great significance is the fact that the National Building Code was only published in August 1980.
Certain industrial sectors with the advice and help of the Consumers' Association of Canada and the responsible government departments have requested that deadlines be set and the exclusive use of metric units be compulsory thereafter. This explains, Mr. Speaker, why the Statute Law Metric Conversion Act (Statute Law Amendment 1976) was passed by Parliament and received royal assent in August, 1977. Pursuant to that act, for instance, a modified regulation under the Weights and Measures Act provides that retailers must sell gas by the litre. This conversion was completed by the end of 1980. A similar regulation established pursuant to the Weights and Measures Act provides that furnishings such as wallpapers, carpets, and bedspreads must be advertised and sold only in metric units as of January 1981.
The role of the Metric Commission Canada which will soon celebrate its tenth birthday is to give support to over 16,000 metric system conversion co-ordinators within the industry in the carrying out of their companies' conversion plans according to the sectorial plans and the four-phase investigation, planning, organization and implementation program. The metric labels on prepackaged products like toothpaste or food products such as sugar and salt, were the first visible signs of the metric conversion being in process. Later on, weather bulletins and forecasts started referring to Celsius degrees. Then, in September. 1977, traffic signs began indicating distances in kilometres and speed limits in kilometres per hour, as well as speedometers on new car models.
Many of us, Mr. Speaker, tend to resist any kind of change. Therefore I am glad to note that since metrication has been introduced Canadians' response has been very favourable. More and more people support this program as they get better acquainted with the new metric system and their initial fears are dispelled. The fact is that metrication has been gently phased in. Since the new temperature units were introduced in 1975, every stage of the conversion program has been preceded by a cooling-off period to allow people to become thoroughly familiar with the process until further changes were made. In their daily life, most Canadians will only need four basic metric units, metres for distance, litres for volume, kilograms for mass and Celsius degrees for temperature. The last stage, namely implementation, will soon be 60 per cent completed. Most Canadians are getting used to metric units as various sectors of our economy implement their conversion plans.

January 29, 1982
Metrication
For instance, the conversion of scales in the food retail trade is a significant metric development for all Canadians. As regards the general public, it is the most important step in the conversion program to the metric system in Canada. In other areas of our economy that conversion is essential as it is carried out in accordance with the objectives of the metric policy of the Government of Canada.
As I said earlier, food stores will continue with the conversion of their scales into metric units, and this was started on January 4, 1982, in the larger cities in Canada. Sales and promotional activities with respect to individually weighed food products in the stores will be converted over a period of two years according to a carefully conceived and planned schedule. Individual schedules have been prepared by 19 district committees in all areas in Canada, those committees being made up of well over 400 volunteers from the food retail trade, the Canadian Consumers' Association, the scales industry, Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada and the Metric Commission of Canada. They are co-ordinating their efforts in order to convert the scales at the retail store level with a minimum of costs and inconveniences. Regulations on weights and measures as applied by Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada have delineated 100 geographical areas in Canada and established their respective schedules.
Mr. Speaker, may I recall that we have decided upon metrication because we want to promote the export of Canadian products. And we all know that exporting our products means creating jobs for Canadians. We are largely dependent in this country upon the export trade to make a living and to maintaining our standard of living which is envied all around the world. Indeed, 31 cents out of each Canadian dollar come from exports. By converting to the metric system we will join 99.8 per cent of the world countries which have already adopted that system or are in the process of doing so. This should level the barriers which are created in a world where people work under two weights and measures systems and that could prevent Canada from improving its export trade with United States and the rest of the world.
I am speaking, of course, on behalf of Canadian agriculture and I know my friends opposite, those who spoke before me, are staunch supporters of Canadian agriculture. For many
years, I had the opportunity to discuss and meet with farmers, and I have yet to meet a farmer from my riding, my area, my province who told me that the new metric system caused him problems. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, the farmers I meet, and as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture I meet many of them, teach me a lot about metrication. They know that system by heart, they have no problem in talking about 2,000 metric tons. And as I said at the outset of my speech, on this side of the House we legislate for the present and the future, and the future is our youth.
Of course, I repeat that it might be somewhat difficult for our generation to use the metric system but I urge the hon. members opposite to go and meet young people and ask them if they have any problems with the metric system. Mr. Speaker, that is why we cannot find any valid reason to support this motion.

subtopic: PROPOSED MORATORIUM AND REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise to speak on the motion put forward by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) concerning the metric conversion program.
The motion recommends that tens of thousands of Canadians stop the work they have voluntarily been engaged in for nearly ten years and that a standing committee of the House be set up to restudy why we decided to go metric in 1970. If I may, I would like to describe the nature of our national program in order to illustrate that the time for asking, "why go metric" has really passed, and that this is not a program which the Government of Canada can turn on and off like a tap without serious disruptions occurring in the marketplace.
